claims.text: The target material is a quaternary equiatomic single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy.
The target alloy has a chemically disordered lattice with high configurational entropy.
The target alloy contains a high density of lattice distortions.
Above 0.5 Tm, the yield strength will become insensitive to strain rate.
Elevated-temperature rate insensitivity results from thermally activated cross-slip locking dominating over dislocation nucleation.
At cryogenic temperatures, the yield strength will be highly rate-sensitive.
Cryogenic deformation is controlled by nano-twinning and stacking-fault formation.
At elevated temperatures, thermal activation enhances screw-dislocation mobility and permits cross-slip over lattice friction.
At low temperatures, a high Peierls barrier prevents cross-slip and forces deformation through twinning or stacking-fault formation.
The strain-rate sensitivity will change from m greater than 0.05 at cryogenic temperatures to approximately zero at elevated temperatures.
The rate-sensitivity transition will correlate with a change from twin-dominated deformation to dislocation-glide-dominated deformation.
Slip and deformation twinning have previously been observed as principal deformation mechanisms in an equiatomic FCC CoCrFeMnNi HEA between 25 °C and 600 °C.
Conventional FCC alloys generally exhibit moderate strain-rate sensitivity across all temperatures because deformation occurs by simple dislocation glide.
In refractory BCC HEAs, screw-dislocation mobility is the primary rate-limiting process at all temperatures.
An FCC-to-HCP transformation could invalidate the proposed deformation mechanism.
Significant precipitation, including TiO precipitation in NbMoTaWVTi, could invalidate the hypothesis.
Chemical short-range ordering affects screw-dislocation rates in BCC refractory HEAs.
The transition temperature is uncertain because the quaternary alloy's stacking-fault energy and the effects of chemical short-range ordering are not specified.
At 600 K, observing m greater than 0.05 despite thermally activated dislocation structures would falsify the predicted rate-insensitive regime.
Observation of deformation dominated by an FCC-to-HCP phase transformation rather than dislocation glide or cross-slip would falsify the proposed mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes rate insensitivity to dominant cross-slip locking, whereas the mechanism says cross-slip enhances screw-dislocation mobility and allows dislocations to overcome lattice friction. It does not reconcile the obstructive locking process with the proposed mobility enhancement.
